What pitch and melody means here: Melody is an organized line of pitches heard across time; contour is the shape made by its rises, falls, and repeated tones. How the relationship changes the result: Stepwise motion often connects smoothly, leaps create sharper contrast, and repetition helps the listener recognize a phrase or arrival. Choice and tradeoff: A narrow range can feel unified but limit contrast. A wide range adds drama but may be harder to sing, play, or track accurately. Worked example: C D E G | E D C creates a rise, a high arrival, and a return; arrows or numbered steps preserve the same contour without an instrument. Non-example: Naming pitch letters without preserving their order does not show melodic contour. 1. ATTACHED MANUEL ACADEMY LEARNER RESOURCE

Resource ID: ma-resource:ma-g5-arts-and-music-u03-l02

Lesson focus: pitch and melody

Resource type: ACADEMY_ORIGINAL_MODEL

MODEL A — “One relationship at a time.” Melody is an organized line of pitches heard across time; contour is the shape made by its rises, falls, and repeated tones. Stepwise motion often connects smoothly, leaps create sharper contrast, and repetition helps the listener recognize a phrase or arrival. Worked example for pitch and melody: C D E G | E D C creates a rise, a high arrival, and a return; arrows or numbered steps preserve the same contour without an instrument. Starting state: state the intended effect, question, or criterion before acting. First decision: locate pitch direction, interval size, contour, phrase, repetition, arrival, and tonal centre. Intermediate state: complete one bounded study, loop, map, or comparison while most features stay stable. Check: cite what changed before judging it. Finished or intentionally partial result: keep the evidence even when it challenges the first intention. Common misapplication: Naming pitch letters without preserving their order does not show melodic contour. Legitimate variation: another learner may choose different comfortable pitch or symbol set, sound or silent notation route, contour, phrase length, final expressive change and still meet the criterion. Use it to study pitch and melody; describe evidence before judging and adapt the demonstrated relationship rather than copying a finished work.

How to use it: Use the attached Manuel Academy resource in this package. It gives you the model, example, or help sheet needed for this task.

Rights: Manuel Academy original; licensed CC BY 4.0 for learner use and adaptation. No third-party text, image, score, lyric, melody, recording, or performance is included.

Specialized art materials, instruments, paid software, cameras, microphones, and recording devices are optional and never affect credit.

presentation_and_privacy.presentation_options: You choose the audience. Keeping the work entirely to yourself, showing it to one parent or trusted adult, or submitting it as a file with no one watching are all full-credit options. No public performance, exhibition, class presentation, live audience, photograph, camera, or voice recording is required at any point in this task, and choosing the most private option never lowers the score.
presentation_and_privacy.text_or_no_audio_alternative: A written alternative is always available for spoken reflection, explanation, or critique and scores the same. Tap, point through, gesture, or use the supplied notation or event map without recording. A written or notated response can show structure and reasoning; it does not claim hearing or performed control that was not actually demonstrated. No instrument, microphone, camera, or public performance is required.

copyright_and_authorship: The graded submission must be your own authorship. A parent, tutor, or AI tool may explain an idea, demonstrate a technique, or give feedback on a draft, but must not produce, write, debug, or make any part of the work that is scored. Any material you did not create yourself must be in the public domain, openly licensed, or used as a short cited excerpt for study — reproduce no more than the point requires, credit the maker and the source, and never copy full lyrics, a complete score, or a whole image and present it as your own.
accessibility_options: Provide readable text plus optional audio or read-aloud support; no voice feature is required.
Chunk directions into one action at a time and show a worked example or model.
Allow typed, handwritten, spoken, drawn, manipulatives-based, or demonstrated responses when the standard permits.
Offer reduced-copying, extended-time, hidden-timer, movement-break, and low-distraction options.
Use captions, alt text, high-contrast print, keyboard access, and text-only fallbacks for media.
Preserve the learning target while adjusting quantity, pacing, representation, or response mode.
task_accessibility_provisions: This task uses sound (pitch and melody). You do not have to hear it to do it. You may use a written or drawn version, feel the beat by tapping or watching, or read the notes on paper instead.
Anything you have to study will also come as plain text, a described version, or a version you can touch.
You can take a break, stretch, or come back to this later. That does not lower your score.
safety_and_privacy_rules: Allow a pause, break, or alternate response mode without treating it as failure.
Protect hearing, ventilation, tool safety, copyright, cultural context, and respectful representation.
Provide a non-performance or low-audience option when needed without lowering the academic target.

media.fallback: Count, point through, tap, speak, gesture, or read the complete pulse and pitch map silently; no instrument, speaker, microphone, or recording is required.

remediation: Route 1: Reduce pitch and melody to three locatable events, areas, steps, or decisions. Label the intended effect beside each and underline the one pitch direction relationship that should carry it. Use a separate small study, four-event loop, thumbnail, evidence table, or paper plan. The adult may model the noticing process on different material but may not change the learner’s work. Check yourself: Point to or name the exact pitch direction evidence before deciding whether it serves the intent. New attempt: Put the support away and make a new arrangement, passage, response, or plan; record what the new evidence shows. Route 2: Return to the last understandable state. Hold every relationship steady except one chosen feature from pitch direction, interval size, contour, phrase, repetition, arrival, and tonal centre; predict what that single change should do. Test the feature on scrap paper, a silent count, a two-event rehearsal loop, movable shapes, or a short evidence sentence before changing the scored work. Check yourself: Name what stayed the same, what changed, and the first observable result—without using “better” as the evidence. New attempt: Create a different small case using the same one-variable method, then transfer the finding to the original task only if it serves the learner’s intent.
extension: Apply pitch and melody under a new constraint, compare two approaches or perspectives, or teach the idea with an original example without completing another learner’s graded work. Treat this as optional depth on pitch and melody rather than extra volume: one harder case done well beats three more of the same. Extension work stays private by default and uses only original, public-domain, or properly cited material. Extension work is never required to reach mastery and must not be assigned as a penalty.
